messages.author: 12f269733c6eb9a2
messages.subject: Re: Distance from "the line",
parts:
Hi Linda:

The perpendicular distance used for your analysis is the distance from
the object to the *line*. This means that you know where the line is
located during your surveying.

It is not necessary for you to stay on the transect line during your
survey. Have a look at Figure 3 in "Field trials of line transect
methods applied to estimation of desert tortoise abundance" Anderson et
al. J. Wildlife Mgmt 65:583-597 in 2001. If you have access to Jstor
(http://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/3803111)

The figure shows a search pattern in which one of the observers weaves
on either side of the transect line while another stays on the line.
Perfectly acceptable. What is not acceptable is missing animals
directly on the line.


On 27/07/2012 09:43, Reinhold, Linda wrote:
> > G'day Distance samplers,
> >
> > On line transects, is the perpendicular distance to an animal taken from the predetermined "line", or from where you happen to be at the time of sighting?? I've had conflicting statistical advice on this.
> >
> > (We spotlight for ground-dwelling marsupials on islands. Our transect lines are marked out by reflective tape, but we only walk them once a year, so some of the markers inevitably fall down and we walk "the line" by GPS until we can see the next reflector post to aim for. This, together with patches of bush that we have to go around rather than through, means we sometimes stray tens of metres off "the line". This also means we could be missing animals on the actual line. I know it would be ideal to walk on "the line" at all times, but it is reality that we don't.)

parts:
Linda, adding to Eric's response, take a look at the duck nest example in c=
hapter 8 of the 2001 distance sampling book. In particular, look at sectio=
n 8.4.3, where it states '... the observer could go around clumps of such v=
egetation ... the measurements must be taken from the transect centreline, =
not to the observer who may be away from the centreline.' This is because =
object density may vary with thickness of vegetation, and if the line meand=
ers to avoid the thicker vegetation, you will get biased estimates.

Steve Buckland
